content.comment_body: Hello to all users of [product_name]. Yesterday, I used my [product_name] start kit together with a display panel for setup. Unfortunately, I wasn't careful and connected a 12/24V module directly to 230V for a brief moment. The 10A fuse blew immediately and the power shut off. After replacing the fuse and properly using the power module, the [product_name] still worked but briefly emitted a bit of smoke and odor, which faded quickly. My question is: Was I simply lucky that the module survived, or does it have some protection feature I missed?

I really hope so. I'm planning more tests over the weekend, and so far nothing seems wrong. I read that grounding may not be needed because of double insulation in [product_name]. Maybe that helped, or maybe it’s unrelated to what happened.

Double insulation isn't related to this issue. The voltage is the key factor here. Supplying 230 VAC to a module designed for 24 VDC is excessive. My guess is that there may be a voltage dependent resistor (VDR) in the power circuit, which might have been destroyed—explaining the smoke.

You're correct—I opened my [product_name] and saw black dust on the back side of the PCB, with some damaged parts that I could clean up. I live in Sweden, so who should I contact for servicing these devices?
Check out this resource for repair services: [url]

Hi [user_name], It's unlikely there's a VDR in a 24VDC module. The voltage regulators have probably failed, and exposure to 230V may have damaged the processor completely. Overall, it sounds like a total loss—repair isn't economical, so purchasing a new device and reloading your backup program is the best option.

Thanks for your response. Yesterday and today, I wrote a simple sequence program and tested all functions using the configuration software and my [product_name] PLC; everything seems to run fine. The web server works and I can connect via IP. Sequence demo: display cycles from white to amber/red and repeats. No issues found so far, maybe Swedish electricity is more stable these days? The only noticeable problem was a mark on the power and relay section of the PCB. All four outputs measure at 24.3V. Time appears to be critical—the brief exposure may have allowed the fuse to respond quickly and save the module. I'll contact [company_name]'s Stockholm office next week.
You really were fortunate! Normally, such an event would destroy the module.
Thank you for sharing this update.
Following my call to the [company_name] Stockholm office, their reply was: 'We do not repair [product_name] devices because they're inexpensive.' Is this policy standard for the whole product line?
I've never been in a repair department, but from what I know, manufacturing a new [product_name] is cheaper than repairing one. Therefore, repairs generally aren't offered.

analysis.insight_summary: The discussion reveals that a [product_name] module unexpectedly survived a brief connection to high voltage, with only minor damage like burn marks and residue inside. Community members pointed out that such incidents usually render the device unusable, and opinions varied on whether protective features or the fuse played a role in its survival. There was some confusion about built-in protection and how the module managed to keep working after the accident.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect the module to offer robust protection against accidental high voltage, provide clear indications of failure or damage, and be somewhat forgiving of setup mistakes. They also value clarity about repair policies and support options from the manufacturer.
